newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland moves to tighen unemployment rules.
newsitem.headline: Poland moves to tighen unemployment rules.

text.p: The Polish government on Monday approved bills tightening rules on unemployment benefits to prevent rampant fraud that costs the national budget billions of zlotys a year, the labour minister said.
The laws will remove loopholes and make it harder to get an unemployment benefit, Andrzej Baczkowski told reporters.

"The current rules are too liberal and are abused. Collecting unemployment benefits must not be a way of life," he said. He said many of the 2.5 million officially jobless either collect benefits illegally because they are secretly working, or only qualify because the law is too lax.
Under the new rules a person would first have to work 270 days to qualify for unemployment benefits. Currently, 180 days of work is required.

Unemployed people who engage in temporary, state- subsidised works would not automatically have the right to benefits. People receiving benefits who are now allowed to take casual jobs paying up to half the minimum wage, would in the future be disqualified if they take any kind of work.
By law, people who lose their jobs are eligible for unemployment benefits of nearly 300 zlotys gross ($110) a month for 12 months. The average monthly salary is 920 zlotys.
Baczkowski said that, if the new regulations became law, the national budget spending for unemployment benefits would be cut by 420 million zlotys next year.
Most of the sum would be spent on creating new jobs and on vocational trainings, he added.
The legisative package will now go to parliament as urgent and is likely to be approved by the end of the year. It should become effective in mid-1997, Baczkowski said.
